generatedBy: Written by Claude from the engine facts, then checked by code. The model explains. It does not decide.

normal|priceOnly|charge|12-15.text: This is where following price alone goes wrong. Power is cheapest from 12 PM to 4 PM, about $17 per MWh, so the plan charges 36 MWh as fast as it can, up to 9.9 MWh in an hour. Grid draw reaches 85.3 MW, 5.8 MW over the 79.5 MW limit, because the substation is already carrying 75.5 MW at 2 PM before the battery adds anything.

normal|clean|discharge|5-6.text: 5 AM is the dirtiest hour of the day in this forecast, about 700 kg of CO2 per MWh, because the grid leans on coal and gas before sunrise. The battery discharges 15 MWh here to push that power off the grid. Price is only about $37 per MWh, so this move is about carbon, not money.

derate|aware|charge|9-10.text: With the limit cut to 71.6 MW the battery gets a narrow window to refill. It takes in 9 MWh over 9 AM to 11 AM, at about $21 per MWh, and grid draw is held to the limit so charging does not make the derate worse.

derate|priceOnly|charge|12-15.text: This is the failure the derate exposes. Load without the battery is already 73.7 MW or more from 12 PM to 4 PM, above the 71.6 MW limit. Price alone still says charge, about $17 per MWh, so the plan adds 36 MWh of charging and grid draw reaches 85.3 MW, 13.8 MW over the limit.

derate|clean|charge|18-20.text: To end the day half full, the battery refills 17 MWh from 6 PM to 9 PM while prices are near $52 per MWh. Grid draw peaks at 71.4 MW, 0.2 MW under the limit. Charging in the evening rush is the cost of keeping the substation safe at midday.
